content: The guideline titled Preventive Chemotherapy to Control Soil-Transmitted Helminth Infections in At-Risk Population Groups was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2017. It provides updated recommendations for the use of preventive chemotherapy as a public health intervention to control soil-transmitted helminth (STH) infections in populations at risk. This document supersedes previous recommendations and complements operational guidance provided in earlier WHO publications. The guideline was developed following rigorous procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. It includes evidence that informed the recommendations, expanded sections on dissemination, and ethical and equity considerations. These updates are based on the most recent reviews of these topics. The guideline defines key terms used within the document. For example, adolescence refers to the period of human growth and development between the ages of 10 and 19. Anthelmintic refers to medicines used to kill helminths (worms) and facilitate their expulsion from the human body. The most commonly used anthelmintics for treating intestinal worm infections in children are benzimidazoles, such as albendazole and mebendazole. The guideline also introduces the concept of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), which measure the number of healthy years lost due to a disease. This metric is used to assess the public health burden of diseases, including STH infections. The document highlights the importance of identifying ineligible populations, such as children under one year of age and pregnant women in their first trimester, who are not qualified to receive anthelmintic treatment due to insufficient evidence of safety. It also discusses the intensity of infection, which refers to the number of helminths infecting an individual, measured either directly (by counting expelled worms) or indirectly (by counting helminth eggs in feces). WHO classifies STH infections as light, moderate, or heavy based on the number of eggs excreted. Morbidity is defined as the clinical consequences of infections and diseases that negatively impact human health. Morbidity from STH infections is often subtle, such as malabsorption or stunted growth, and is proportional to the worm burden. Moderate or heavy infections are typically responsible for significant morbidity. The guideline identifies specific population groups, such as preschool children (aged 24 to 59 months) and young children (aged 12 to 23 months), as key targets for preventive chemotherapy interventions. It also defines prevalence of any soil-transmitted helminth infection as the percentage of individuals in a population infected with at least one species of STH. The guideline acknowledges the contributions of various WHO departments, technical experts, and external collaborators in its development. It also recognizes the financial support provided by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Nutrition International, and the International Micronutrient Malnutrition Prevention and Control Program of the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The document emphasizes that donors do not influence the guideline development process, including the formulation of research questions, systematic reviews, or recommendations. It also includes a glossary of terms to ensure clarity and consistency in the interpretation of the guideline. In summary, this guideline serves as a comprehensive resource for health professionals and program managers to implement preventive chemotherapy interventions effectively, with the ultimate goal of reducing the burden of soil-transmitted helminth infections in at-risk populations.
